title: Building an AI-Forward Law Firm: Lessons from Quinn Emanuel — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Reeves · Chris Kercher

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not endorse the cluster’s central claim that automation threatens the experience needed to develop future expertise. Instead, it reframes the issue as a practical adoption challenge: lawyers should experiment on real matters, retain human judgment and rigorous verification, and give junior lawyers a central role in checking AI-assisted work. This offers an AI-critical workflow but not the cluster’s proposed reconstruction of apprenticeship through simulation and protected independent practice.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source does not substantively assess whether automation weakens apprenticeship or partner succession. Instead, it shifts the emphasis to practitioner-led adoption and recasts junior lawyers as substantive verifiers of AI-assisted work, offering an alternative operating priority rather than directly supporting the cluster’s pipeline proposition.
qs: It’s not very effective to have people far removed from day-to-day practice dictate, “Here’s exactly how you shall use AI.” Instead, we let the practicing lawyers guide how AI gets implemented in their workflows.

st.t: General platforms: Legal procedure may defend specialists
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that general-purpose AI can become a useful legal-work interface without establishing autonomous practice. It materially develops that view by prescribing matter-specific context, conversational iteration and substantive lawyer verification, while offering only anecdotal—not measured—workflow evidence. Its claim that specialist tools are unnecessary to start adds competitive pressure but does not establish their displacement.
qs: We’ll load it up with the core context – maybe the complaint, the answer, important deposition excerpts, whatever – so Claude has that all in its “brain” when we ask it for something on the case.
In our field, someone should already be carefully cite-checking everything – not just checking the Bluebook formatting for a citation, but the actual substance.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on organisational absorption and materially develops that proposition through a concrete practitioner-led implementation model: practising lawyers identify workflow needs, coaches support experimentation, culture enables adoption, and continued use matters more than initial access. Its reported benefits remain experiential rather than independently quantified.
qs: It’s not very effective to have people far removed from day-to-day practice dictate, “Here’s exactly how you shall use AI.” Instead, we let the practicing lawyers guide how AI gets implemented in their workflows.
It’s one thing to get people signed up or logged in once; it’s another to see them continue to use the tools regularly.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source accepts lawyer-supervised augmentation and materially develops the cluster’s implementation proposition through a practice-led model: lawyers test AI on live matters, evaluate its usefulness using domain expertise, and retain substantive verification responsibility. Its reported productivity and quality gains are practitioner observations rather than quantified evidence, and it does not resolve the wider staffing or junior-development tension.
qs: It’s not very effective to have people far removed from day-to-day practice dictate, “Here’s exactly how you shall use AI.” Instead, we let the practicing lawyers guide how AI gets implemented in their workflows.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers

Its reported broad uptake illustrates how organisational culture and workflow adoption—not autonomous delivery alone—can drive practical AI use, though it provides little evidence on pricing or market restructuring.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Quinn Emanuel accepts the cluster’s framing of AI adoption as organisational change and materially develops it with a practitioner-led implementation model: frontline lawyers identify concrete workflow problems, while dedicated staff provide training, culture-building and tool evaluation. Its voluntary experimentation, verification guardrails and reported uptake offer a practical example, though productivity and quality effects remain anecdotal rather than causally measured.

st.an: The source supports selective AI augmentation by treating routine brainstorming as suitable for delegation while retaining human communication skill as central to effective AI use. Its contribution is anecdotal and predictive, however, and it does not address the cluster’s concerns about verification costs, developmental loss or independent competence assessment.

st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: The source supports selective, practical learning rather than exhaustive release chasing: participants use a small set of expert commentators, podcasts, newsletters and AI-assisted explanations to stay informed around existing workloads. Its claims are experience-based and optimistic rather than measured, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caveat.
qs: The technology is changing so quickly that by following a few smart thought leaders who get to focus on it full-time (while the rest of us have our full-time jobs), we can take advantage of some great shortcuts.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s practical account of AI adoption: lawyer-led workflow integration, secure enterprise deployment and rigorous human verification are presented as prerequisites for useful adoption. Its reported productivity benefits are practitioner anecdotes rather than comparative evidence, consistent with the cluster’s caution that market-wide effects remain unproven. It does not materially address pricing reform or the broader apprenticeship problem.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s adoption argument by emphasising hands-on experimentation, organisational culture, real-work collaboration and risk awareness. Its framing of AI as a side-by-side helper is consistent with a copilot model, but it provides no measured outcomes and does not substantively address specialist workflow-layer durability or verification practices.
qs: So my approach was, let’s just do it – get it into people’s hands and see what happens – while being mindful of the risks.
Jen and I give a lot of presentations to legal teams (in-house teams, law firms of all sizes), and every organization has its own starting DNA, its own culture.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source directly supports practitioner-led experimentation before technological certainty: practising lawyers shape context-specific workflows with innovation support, while leadership broadens access and encourages iterative use. Its benefits remain anecdotal and unquantified, consistent with the synthesis’s caution that adoption experience does not establish reliability or performance gains.
qs: It’s not very effective to have people far removed from day-to-day practice dictate, “Here’s exactly how you shall use AI.” Instead, we let the practicing lawyers guide how AI gets implemented in their workflows.

Quinn is very AI-forward, and we saw how strong leadership – combined with putting tools in everyone’s hands and fostering an experimental, optimistic mindset – has led to a lot of interesting uses for AI.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source endorses sustained AI learning through experimentation, expert commentary, podcasts and peer exchange, while anticipating better client service and more enjoyable practice. This aligns directly with the cluster’s engagement-first agenda, though the claims remain experiential and prospective rather than measured evidence of effectiveness.
qs: It’s been such a fun conversation, and I’m really, really grateful to both of you for coming on — and grateful to Quinn for fostering such a great culture that allows this kind of experimentation.

This conversation is a great example of optimistic, positive thinking about how this technology is going to make not only better services for your clients, but — and what really came through for me — a more fun, more enjoyable practice.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source endorses the cluster’s supervised-AI model: solo and small-practice lawyers may use AI for assistance and review, but remain responsible for the work and must strengthen human verification where independent review is unavailable. It also treats confidentiality safeguards as a prerequisite. Its recommendation to adopt rapidly once controls are established does not substantively reject the cluster’s caution about verification burdens.
qs: Still, it’s on you as the attorney to be extra careful.
But if not, then double down on your own verification steps.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition that legal AI is best deployed as a human-led copilot rather than a wholesale substitute for lawyers. Its cautious pilots, internal education and low-friction use cases also align with selective deployment and organisational adoption, though it offers mainly experiential rather than systematic evidence and gives limited attention to verification burdens or jagged task performance.
qs: It doesn’t replace your own judgment or creativity, but it amplifies them.

But early on, yes, it was uncertain territory and we proceeded cautiously: “Let’s try this, but take a lot of precautions so that if something goes wrong, we can catch it and fix it going forward.”  Now, fast forward to today – we’ve gotten a ton of traction.

st.t: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
st.an: Kercher supports treating trust as a workflow property: hallucinations remain real, but human verification, training and risk-mitigation processes can make AI usable without requiring error-free output. His voluntary, hands-on adoption model also reinforces the cluster’s emphasis on organisational change, though his evidence is experiential rather than quantitative.
qs: Once we got over that hump and put in place processes to mitigate those risks (and frankly, as people became more savvy about the limitations), I felt more comfortable.

kp.k: Bottom-up experimentation drives Quinn's reported AI adoption
kp.d: Chris Kercher describes an initially informal, voluntary rollout beginning with young associates, staff and anticipated early adopters. The QE Skunkworks program supported experimentation through Slack and Zoom without credit or billable time. He reports hundreds of firm users, attributing adoption to access, shared learning and enthusiasm rather than a management mandate.
qs: I think we’ve now got hundreds of people at the firm using AI.
We started from the bottom up – we began with young associates, staff members, people I thought would be early tech adopters who’d use it responsibly and share their learnings.
There was no credit or billable time given; it was just, “If you want to learn about this, mess around with it, and share your findings, join in.”

kp.k: Dedicated innovation counsel sustains implementation alongside legal practice
kp.d: Kercher says his litigation practice prevented him from running adoption full-time, prompting the hiring of Jen Reeves to handle training, culture-building and tool assessment. He characterizes dedicated implementation capacity as a primary pillar of the approach and the firm's most valuable intervention.
qs: I also asked if we could hire someone to run this operation full-time – someone to handle training, culture-building, evaluating new tools, etc.
hiring Jen has been the single most valuable thing we’ve done.
That’s become a primary pillar of our approach, as it turns out.

kp.k: Enterprise access and human verification underpin experimentation
kp.d: Kercher and Reeves describe enterprise arrangements as their response to confidentiality concerns and substantive human checking as their response to fabricated AI output. Kercher acknowledges encountering fabricated quotations or facts in internal drafts and emphasizes verification of underlying substance, not merely citation formatting. These are reported safeguards, not demonstrated elimination of risk.
qs: Let’s make sure everything that leaves the firm with our name on it has been cite-checked and rigorously reviewed (as it’s supposed to be anyway).
We drill into our users: verify everything.
I’ve been burned a few times in internal drafts where I thought I had a great quote or fact, and it turned out the model just fabricated it.
Instead, we addressed the risks in other ways (like the enterprise solution and training on verification) so that people can genuinely experiment and integrate AI without a huge overhead.

kp.k: Junior lawyers retain responsibility for grounding legal output
kp.d: Kercher presents junior attorneys as human verifiers who ensure AI-assisted work corresponds to actual case law and facts. His account assigns them an important quality-control role within assisted drafting rather than claiming AI removes their responsibilities.
qs: So, junior attorneys – suddenly they become masters of reality in this process.
They’re the ones making sure everything we say aligns with something real: case law, facts, what have you.

kp.k: Training centers on actual matters, not prescribed workflows
kp.d: Reeves argues that practicing lawyers should guide workflow integration because they possess the relevant subject-matter expertise. Initial instruction covers tool operation, but subsequent consultations address live problems. Kercher explains that concrete matters allow lawyers to assess whether outputs are useful or merely repeat what they already know.
qs: Instead, we let the practicing lawyers guide how AI gets implemented in their workflows.
I’m here to show you how to use this tool and help brainstorm ideas, but you have to tell me what you’re working on.
But the real magic happens when they come back to us while working on an actual project.
But in each case, they’re actively evaluating it on something concrete.

kp.k: Voluntary onboarding develops into colleague-driven demand
kp.d: Kercher describes initially avoiding a firm-wide launch or forced adoption, using one-on-one training, partner updates and an internal mailing list instead. Reeves reports moving from recruiting users for a few licenses to receiving at least five daily requests for access or ideas. Kercher says the remaining common obstacle is lack of time and focuses on quick, approachable wins; these are practitioner accounts rather than systematically reported engagement data.
qs: Because, to be fair, we didn’t have a top-down mandate or formal policy at first – we were just doing it organically.
If someone isn’t comfortable with it, that’s fine – we’re not shoving it down anyone’s throat.
Now I’m getting at least five requests a day (often more) from people who want access or have an idea, especially whenever we send a newsletter or one of us mentions something in a meeting.
The more common stance I encounter now is a sort of FOMO with a dash of guilt: lawyers saying, “I know I need to try this… I just haven’t had time.”

kp.k: General models currently meet substantial practice needs
kp.d: Reeves says Quinn is primarily using general models rather than specialized legal AI tools. Kercher describes Claude's writing and editing as his initial catalyst and reports a recent ChatGPT pilot alongside Claude. He recommends careful product selection because many emerging products do not serve the firm's needs; Reeves advises smaller firms not to regard expensive legal-specific software as a prerequisite.
qs: We recently started a ChatGPT pilot to complement our Claude pilot, so now we have many folks trying out both models at all levels of the firm.
That’s basically all we’re using at Quinn right now – we haven’t even needed fancy specialized legal AI tools yet, because the frontier models are that capable.
And so a lot of products appeared that don’t really serve our needs.
I wanted to make sure we were smart about what we buy, and that we had enough bandwidth to look at everything carefully before adopting it.

kp.k: Institutional knowledge retrieval remains an exploratory workstream
kp.d: Kercher identifies the firm's difficult-to-access, organize and classify information as a third strategic focus alongside adoption and tool selection. He describes exploration of AI for understanding the firm's business and practices, not a completed deployment with measured outcomes.
qs: Quinn Emanuel has a lot of information about itself and what we do, but historically it’s hard to access and hard to organize or classify.
So we’ve started exploring whether we can use AI tools to better understand our own business and practices – to unearth institutional knowledge that’s been hard to tap into.

kp.k: AI-assisted drafting reportedly improves speed, quality and enjoyment
kp.d: Kercher recounts producing a client summary on a Friday before a holiday weekend and says it was easier and higher quality than the team's alternative process. He reports faster, more creative work and greater professional enjoyment. These are qualitative experiences, including his comparison with other firms' likely turnaround, without quantified productivity or quality testing.
qs: We cranked out a summary for a client on a Friday afternoon before a holiday weekend – something most firms wouldn’t have gotten to until the next week.
But we did it; it was beautiful, informative, and correct. And it was both easier and higher quality.
We’re able to move faster and be more creative.
Honestly, this is the most exciting time I’ve ever had practicing law.

kp.k: Small practices can amplify capacity, subject to safeguards
kp.d: Kercher recommends that solos first address confidentiality through appropriate privacy arrangements or offline models, then experiment with supervised drafting, planning and review. He notes the particular risk of lacking a second human reviewer: AI can partly assist, but attorney responsibility remains, with a part-time lawyer or law student suggested for critical checking where feasible.
qs: Honestly, I think it’s a fantastic time to be a solo or in a small firm, precisely because AI lets you leverage yourself so much more.
First, address the non-negotiables like client data and confidentiality.
Second, recognize the potential pitfall that as a solo you don’t have a second pair of eyes on everything.
If you can swing it, maybe hire a part-time young lawyer or even a law student intern to be a second human checker for critical outputs – just like any quality control.
But if not, then double down on your own verification steps.

kp.k: Matter context and clear communication guide effective use
kp.d: Kercher and Reeves recommend matter-specific conversations containing core documents, facts and issues, followed by natural-language requests and iteration. Kercher reports that relevant context substantially improves outputs and suggests asking the model how it can assist with a workflow. He expects lawyers' communication skills to transfer to AI use; neither speaker presents formal prompt-performance measurements.
qs: One practical tip: set up a “project” chat with the AI for each matter.
We’ll load it up with the core context – maybe the complaint, the answer, important deposition excerpts, whatever – so Claude has that all in its “brain” when we ask it for something on the case.
Just explain what you need in plain language, provide the context, and iterate.
Because if you can communicate really clearly to a human—a judge, or whoever—I have a feeling you’re going to be able to communicate well with the AI.

kp.k: Deep Research supports internal inquiries and client preparation
kp.d: Reeves describes responding to firm-wide requests for information by using o3 to develop a research prompt, then passing it to Deep Research and forwarding the resulting dossier. She reports faster preparation for a general counsel conversation while emphasizing that the partner still conducts the call. The workflow also exposes colleagues to potential AI applications.
qs: Basically, we use o3 to come up with a research prompt and pull out anything that might be helpful.
We feed that into our Deep Research tool, and it comes back with an amazing dossier, which we forward to the partner who asked.
It helped me prepare — I had intelligent things to say to this GC that I wouldn’t necessarily have thought of on my own.
So again, you’re still the partner doing the call, but it helps you prepare so much faster.

kp.k: Improved communication could surface previously unarticulated legal problems
kp.d: Responding to a host's five- or ten-year question, Kercher speculates that AI may improve ordinary interactions rather than radically automate life. He proposes that helping businesspeople clarify intent could overcome reluctance to engage with legal issues and surface problems previously left unraised. He uses communication with medical specialists as an analogy and explicitly leaves practical outcomes uncertain.
qs: I think we may reach a world where, forget agents and automating life… life may look relatively the same—except it’ll be better.

But if you open up the ability of people to just get a little bit more clear in their thoughts, and be able to organize it better, suddenly they may come up with entirely new legal problems that never would’ve been raised.
We’ll see how that works in practice.

kp.k: Hosts connect adoption to organizational innovation theory
kp.d: Bridget McCormack interprets Quinn's approach through Ethan Mollick's crowd, lab and leader model: end-user participation, a dedicated experimentation group and leadership support. Kercher acknowledges reading Mollick but says he did not consciously implement a particular article as a plan. The connection is a host's framework interpretation with guest acknowledgment of influence, not an independently tested explanation of Quinn's results.
qs: You have the crowd (everybody “in”), which I think is exactly the right approach because only the end-users know the best ways AI can impact their workflow.
You have the Skunkworks lab team that’s really driving experimentation. And you have firm leadership not only supporting it but investing in it.
It’s not like I sat down with an Ethan Mollick article and decided, “This is our plan.”
But I’m not surprised we ended up following his advice, because I’ve been reading his work since the beginning.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Chris Kercher claims AI enables faster, easier and higher-quality client work while supporting greater creativity.
pts.d: Kercher describes Claude as a capable writer and editor and reports that his teams can deliver work more quickly. His concrete example is a client summary completed on a Friday before a holiday weekend, which he says most firms would not have delivered until the next week. He also mentions using AI in a case resulting in a trial-court victory, without claiming that AI caused the victory. These are accounts of lawyer-supervised assistance, not autonomous delivery of legal services.

pts.k: Kercher and Jen Reeves claim voluntary experimentation, practice-specific support and dedicated innovation leadership encourage sustained AI adoption.
pts.d: Kercher credits tool access, peer learning through QE Skunkworks and Reeves's full-time training and culture-building role with the firm's adoption. Reeves argues that practicing lawyers should shape implementation rather than receive a rigid workflow prescribed by people removed from practice. They describe adoption expanding from an interested cross-section of associates and staff to users at all levels. Reeves says enterprise access and verification training reduce the friction that extensive upfront redaction would otherwise create. Their claims concern the experience of Quinn Emanuel rather than a demonstrated universal adoption formula.

pts.k: Kercher presents human verification as a continuing requirement of AI-assisted legal work and a consequential role for junior lawyers.
pts.d: Kercher argues that AI's fabricated quotations, citations and facts should be addressed through substantive checking and rigorous review rather than treated as a reason to reject AI altogether. He describes junior attorneys as ensuring that assertions correspond to actual law and facts. He reports encountering fabricated material in internal drafts. Enterprise access is presented as the firm's response to confidentiality concerns, while verification addresses output reliability; these are separate safeguards in his account.

pts.k: Kercher claims AI can amplify solo and small-firm lawyers' capacity and partly compensate for limited colleague support.
pts.d: Kercher says AI can help small practices organize work, develop arguments and draft routine documents while the lawyer supervises and edits. He describes AI as partially filling a second-reader or thought-partner gap, but emphasizes that it does not remove the attorney's responsibility. He recommends a second human checker for critical outputs where feasible, or stronger personal verification otherwise. This is advice extrapolated from his own experience, not a reported study of solo-practice outcomes or an assertion that AI replaces human quality control.

pts.k: Reeves and Kercher claim general-purpose frontier models already support substantial legal work, especially when supplied with relevant matter context.
pts.d: Reeves says Quinn is essentially using general models such as Claude and ChatGPT rather than needing specialized legal-AI products at this stage. She argues that smaller firms need not acquire expensive legal-specific software to begin. Kercher reports that matter-specific documents and facts substantially improve output, and both speakers favor clear natural-language communication and iteration over elaborate prompting. Kercher also suggests lawyers' existing communication skills transfer to working with AI. These claims do not establish that general models meet every legal need or outperform specialist products.

pts.k: Reeves claims Deep Research accelerates background research and helps lawyers prepare more effectively for client conversations.
pts.d: Reeves describes responding to firm-wide requests for information by using o3 to develop a research prompt, running it through Deep Research and sending the resulting dossier to the requesting partner. She says this has demonstrated AI's usefulness internally and helped her prepare substantive points for a general counsel conversation. The lawyer still conducts the call; AI assists preparation. No measured time saving or independent assessment of dossier quality is provided.

pts.k: Kercher identifies unlocking the firm's institutional knowledge as an exploratory AI opportunity.
pts.d: Kercher says Quinn has substantial information about its business and practices that has historically been difficult to access, organize or classify. The firm is exploring whether AI can make that information more usable. This is an initiative and prospective capability, not a reported completed system or demonstrated business result.

pts.k: Kercher speculates that AI-assisted communication could help business clients articulate concerns and surface legal problems that previously went unraised.
pts.d: In response to a question about looking back in five or ten years, Kercher envisages improvements in communication and idea generation rather than necessarily wholesale agent-driven automation. He suggests that businesspeople who currently disengage when matters appear legal could use AI to clarify their thinking and raise additional legal issues. His prediction is tentative and does not quantify additional demand, revenue or access-to-justice effects.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is the interviewees' firsthand experience, illustrative work examples and limited self-reported adoption indicators.
pts.d: Kercher and Reeves support present-tense claims with their Quinn experience: a holiday-weekend client summary, research dossiers, hands-on onboarding, context-rich matter chats and encounters with fabricated content in internal drafts. Adoption indicators are Kercher's estimate of hundreds of users and Reeves's report of at least five daily access requests or ideas. Reeves mentions engagement numbers but does not disclose retention rates or usage-series data. The transcript supplies no controlled comparisons, benchmarks, measured productivity or cost reductions, or independently assessed client outcomes. References to Mollick and Karpathy explain influences on their approach, rather than supplying specific empirical findings establishing the legal-service claims. The institutional-knowledge initiative is exploratory, and the future communication claim is explicitly speculative.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims concern current practice in the 2025 interview after roughly a year of experimentation; benefits are conditional on confidentiality protections, verification, relevant context and user learning.
pts.d: Kercher dates initial experimentation and the Claude enterprise initiative approximately a year before the interview, and describes a recently added ChatGPT pilot. He reports that model outputs have become more impressive and reliable over that period, without providing comparative measurements. He and Reeves condition responsible use on addressing client-data concerns and checking outputs, while recognizing that some experiments fail. For solos, Kercher suggests enterprise or other privacy-protective options, potentially offline models for sensitive information, and extra human checking. These are his recommended safeguards, not demonstrated guarantees of confidentiality or privilege preservation. Institutional-knowledge work has begun but has no completion date. The communication prediction follows a five-to-ten-year question, but Kercher does not commit to that deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed changes primarily affect practicing lawyers, junior verifiers, innovation staff, small practices and business clients.
pts.d: At Quinn, partners, associates and staff gain drafting, research, organization and brainstorming assistance; junior attorneys retain a substantive verification role. A dedicated innovation lawyer supports training, tool assessment and experimentation. Solo and small-firm practitioners are presented as potential beneficiaries of greater individual capacity, but face particular quality-control challenges without colleagues. Clients may receive faster and better-prepared work, while businesspeople may become better able to articulate legal concerns. Kercher also describes greater personal enjoyment in practice. The interviewees do not offer concrete predictions of lawyer headcount reductions, altered staffing structures, changed billing models, quantified market-share shifts or improved access to justice.
